title_en: Ocarina of Time Is More Than a Nostalgia Trip – It Proves Nintendo’s Family Friendly Days Are Still Going Strong, Even 20 Years After It Launched the Wii
summary_en: Ocarina of Time revisits Nintendo's past in multiple ways, echoing not just its N64 origins, but the wonderful family-focused era of the Wii, which celebrates its 20th anniversary this week.
body_en:
This is an opinion piece from writer Jess Kinghorn. IGN's opinion columns represent the personal viewpoints of the writer, drawing on their own experiences and research to explore the exciting world of video games.
Even on the cusp of GTA 6's record-breaking train pulling out from the station, there's still another locomotive daring to take to the tracks. The Ocarina of Time remake is the criminal sandbox’s polar opposite, and its already broken Switch 2 sales records . It's easy to see why because it's just the latest success sprouting from the platform holder's tried and true strategy – and with the 20th anniversary of the Nintendo Wii on GTA 6 day no less, November 19, those magic beans continue to flourish. Games can be for everyone.
The Switch 2 is humble hardware compared to its console competitors, though The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is no less pretty. As I venture back into the Kokiri forest, witnessing its eternally childlike denizens come to terms with the passing of the Great Deku Tree and stare down the first autumn they’ve ever known, this fairytale has its hooks in me once more. It's what Nintendo is best at, and just goes to show that the studio completely understands how to pitch its family friendly games in a way no other platform holder has successfully managed to leverage.
Exceptions are few and far between. I loved Astro Bot , but that mascot platformer feels like an anomaly on the PlayStation 5. As for Xbox, I’m still a bit nervy about the fate of Banjo Kazooie maker Rare in the platform holder’s hands. The heaviest hitters on either console are more geared towards chasing greater graphical fidelity and technical fire power in order to impress the grown ups ( with a memory supply crisis price to match ). Nintendo has picked a distinctly different path, and it's not as if the Switch 2 is its first time stepping up to the plate.
While Ocarina of Time hails from the N64, and Nintendo’s family friendly approach dates back even further, it's really the humble Wii that set the publisher up for its modern success , ditching HD trends to instead focus on affordable gaming that truly had something for everybody. Rather than chasing the dragon of high fidelity graphics, first-party Nintendo releases focussed on strong art direction, with a case in point being WarioWare: Smooth Moves .
Released a few months after the Wii’s release, this rapidfire series of motion controlled minigames leveraged a blend of 2D and 3D art as its own easy to understand shorthand. Though 3D graphics are used sparingly, their sometimes rough and ready look only adds to the game’s humour. All of that silliness softens the blow of biffing a minigame with a sensible chuckle – precision picking Wario’s nose may be downright juvenile, but I’m no less charmed.
2008’s Animal Crossing: City Folk is less silly, but is similarly playful in its presentation. For instance, the village here looks a bit like Nintendo raided the craft box full of the really fun, patterned paper. While I appreciate New Horizons’ shininess, its strong art direction also makes the most of what the humble Switch 2 hardware has to offer.
Though everything is more expensive these days, I still feel Nintendo trying to resist that pull with the Switch 2. There's also something to be said for how, say, the Ocarina of Time remake sits on the minimal home screen like a doorway to adventure. Conversely, booting up my PS5 or Xbox Series X confronts me with an advertising upsell gauntlet. The Switch 2’s presentation is just one more cue borrowed from the Wii and its charming channel-based UI.
The clue to the Wii's success really is in the name, though a bigger giveaway would be the game library. Wii Sports launched as a pack-in title, offering a series of simplistic minigames to get a broad audience up to speed with its motion controls, while also stoking more than a little healthy competition in living rooms across the globe. Trust me, you’ve not lived until you’ve gone toe to toe at tennis with your Granny after one wine too many during Christmas dinner – those Wiimotes wrist straps really were non-optional.
And if Granny didn’t feel up to defending her tennis title but still wanted to enjoy a spot of seasonal family bonding, there were plenty of other options besides. For instance, 2007’s Super Mario Galaxy is the console at its toyetic best, offering an inviting experience that’s both fun to play as well as watch . There’s plenty of whimsy for all, with the platforming’s gravity effects entertaining players and onlookers alike, though using the motion controls to sniff out collectibles could easily become a group activity too.
Turn the Wii’s controller on its side, however, and New Super Mario Bros. Wii plays with a limited button layout just like the classic 8-bit adventure. With the Joy-Con 2, the more things have changed the more they stay the same.
Link also made an appearance in the Wii’s 21-strong launch line-up with The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess , another game that feels like it was still delivering on that ‘something for everyone’ promise, even as it skewed a bit edgier with its T for Teen rating. For me, it hit at just the right time and now I have the dynamic duo of Link and Midna to thank for my life long love of both werewolves and goth women. And despite not even being a co-op game, I have fond memories of playing it alongside (and arguing with) my baby sister.
Besides, what's easier to understand than waggling to swing a sword? Simplicity of play is a feature not a bug, and it's why going from Ocarina of Time to Twilight Princess to Breath of the Wild back to Ocarina of Time through the remake feels so natural. They've never had much crust to cut in the first place.
It's not as if mature games don't make an appearance on Nintendo consoles. Smart third-party exclusive deals such as No More Heroes or MadWorld on the Wii aren't a stone's throw away from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 finally gracing Switch 2 .
Nintendo’s first-party games, though, continue the Wii’s welcoming ethos. In a world where Fortnite and Roblox are filled to the brim with microtransactions, Nintendo's commitment to delivering worlds that anyone can enjoy simply as they are is refreshing. Whether I'm click-clacking across Switch 2 games, or dusting off the old Wii, remarkably little has changed – like Link pulling out that Master Sword, those 20 years have passed in the blink of an eye.
Jess Kinghorn is a freelancer writer who has written for PC Gamer, PLAY, and GamesRadar+.
